newsitem.title: USA: Congress takes on carnival air before tax vote.
newsitem.headline: Congress takes on carnival air before tax vote.

text.p: Congress took on a circus air Thursday with an event for everyone, from youthful Republicans cheering "Newt! Newt! Newt!" to AIDs activists urging everyone, including lawmakers, to be tested for HIV.

After weeks of busy days and late nights, the House and Senate were both wrestling with a historic tax bill hoping to complete work and take home tax cuts to constituents at the Fourth of July parades.

Before they finished, some of that holiday feeling crept in with a virtual carnival of made-for-television events. In centre stage was a ceremonial re-dedication in the Rotunda of the controversial marble statue of three leaders of the fight for women's suffrage -- formally named the Portrait Monument and informally derided as "Ladies in a Bathtub" because of the way the statues were grouped in a block of stone.

The cavernous room beneath the Capitol dome was packed with an overwhelmingly female audience to hear House Speaker Newt Gingrich and others welcome the statue's return after 76 years stored in the Capitol Crypt.

Less than an hour later, young Republican staffers stopped munching pizza long enough to shout "Newt! Newt! Newt!" and wave signs saying "Thanks for Tax Reform" at the energetic urging of event organisers.

Americans for Tax Reform's Audrey Mullen said she had ordered "enough pizza to feed 600 people or 100 hungry interns." The brief rally in support of tax cuts was held in the usually staid House Ways and Means Committee room, which had been decked out campaign-style with red, white and blue balloons for the event.

Later, under a blazing summer sun, Republican Representative Tom Coburn of Oklahoma and AIDS Action Council's Daniel Zingale, who often oppose each other on AIDS-related issues, held a joint news conference to urge everyone to be tested for HIV, the virus that causes AIDS. The heat, and the press of work in the House, forced them to cancel plans to be tested publicly on the House lawn.

The events took place with a summer tourist season in full swing. Hundreds roamed the Capitol, which serves both as historical museum and modern office building, clogging its hallways and brushing shoulders with congressional leaders as they scurried back and forth from the tax debates.

Wandering into the fray was Australian Prime Minister John Howard who paid morning calls on Gingrich and Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, Republican of Mississippi -- both with photo ops for cameras.
"What have you heard?" was the key question. Its meaning was understood by all as everyone from janitors to senators wondered how late the final Senate vote on the tax bill would occur.
